_comment: SHARED FIXTURE - one answer key for the session subsystem, all four frameworks.
ADR-0024: swapping file for redis, valkey, mongodb, memcached or database
changes ONE env var and NOTHING ELSE. Identical application code, identical
These are INVARIANTS, not a bug list. Six defects were measured here on
2026-08-01 and each is an instance of one of the rules below being broken.
Sessions carry a second weight the other subsystems do not: a session defect
is usually a SECURITY defect. A session that does not expire when told, or one
that silently becomes empty, is an auth outcome rather than a storage one.
HOW THIS IS CHECKED: see scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py. An invariant with
an empty 'cases' list is OWED - declared, not yet proven. A case that was named
and has since disappeared FAILS the build.

invariants.rule: TINA4_SESSION_TTL is honoured by EVERY backend. A session expires when the configured TTL says so, on file, redis, valkey, mongodb, memcached and database alike.
invariants.why: MEASURED: in Ruby the TTL is honoured by the memcached backend ONLY - every other backend hard-codes 86400. An operator setting a 15-minute session gets 24 hours on five of six backends, and nothing reports it. This is a security outcome expressed as a storage default.
cases: session ttl env var expires the record on every backend
session ttl env var keeps a long lived record on every backend
session ttl env var reaches the stored deadline out of band
session ttl option on the session reaches the stored record
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-04 on the lab host (Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64) against a LIVE Redis 7, Valkey 8, memcached 1.6.45, MongoDB 7, PostgreSQL 16 and real SQLite files, TINA4_REQUIRE_SERVICES=1, real wall-clock expiry with no clock mocking anywhere. RE-MEASURED at v3 HEAD before any fix and the defect was still there at the line: Ruby read TINA4_SESSION_TTL in exactly ONE handler (memcached), while file, redis, mongodb and database each hard-coded `@ttl = options[:ttl] || 86400` and valkey read a Ruby-only TINA4_SESSION_VALKEY_TTL; the first run of the new spec went red with 'TINA4_SESSION_TTL=2 was ignored by: file, database, redis, valkey, mongodb' and 'file stored now+86400s, database stored now+86400s, redis stored now+86400s, valkey stored now+86400s'. FOUND AS WELL, and NOT in the original finding: Ruby's Session#save called safe_write(@id, @data) with NO ttl, so an explicit Session.new(ttl:) never reached the store at all - the cookie carried Max-Age and the record did not. Ruby's mongodb handler ALSO had no read-time expiry check, delegating entirely to a TTL index; mongod's TTL monitor sweeps once per 60 SECONDS, so a 2-second session stayed readable for up to a minute past expiry, and it stored updated_at where Python, PHP and Node all store an absolute expires_at. AND Python was broken too, narrowly: FileSessionHandler and DatabaseSessionHandler had no ttl at all, so a bare write(id, data) stored _expires = 0 meaning NEVER EXPIRES while the identical call on memcached expired in an hour - fixed in Python rather than mirrored, per the Python-is-master-unless-Python-is-broken rule. PHP already satisfied the invariant and is a pure lock-in. Node satisfies it end-to-end through Session, which is the only place it reads TINA4_SESSION_TTL for five of six backends; its HANDLER-boundary half is OWED and tracked by ADR-0027, because Node deliberately reads a zero ttl as 'never expires' and pins that with session_mongo_zero_ttl_never_expires - flipping a deliberate, test-locked decision needed an ADR, not a silent change. MUTATION-PROVED in every framework, each mutation asserted to APPLY before running: reverting Ruby's file default kills 2 cases naming 'file' and redis's kills 2 naming redis; removing Ruby's mongo read-time guard kills 1 naming mongodb; reverting Ruby's or Python's save-forwarding kills EXACTLY the Session-level case and nothing else; dropping Python's file or database default kills 2 naming that backend. Recorded because it nearly fooled me: the first Ruby mutation attempt used sed with a `|` delimiter against code containing `||`, silently failed to apply, and reported a meaningless 4-examples-0-failures green - a mutation that does not apply is not a mutation. Python 4772 passed / 27 skipped; Ruby 4908 examples / 0 failures / 8 pending at two different seeds, baseline 4904; PHP 4839 tests / 15295 assertions / 0 failures / 37 skipped; Node 7069 passed / 0 failed across 237 files.

invariants.rule: A TTL is expressed in the same units by the caller regardless of provider, and each backend converts to whatever its wire protocol needs.
invariants.why: MEASURED: memcached treats any TTL above 2592000 seconds (30 days) as an ABSOLUTE UNIX timestamp. A raw TTL above that threshold is read as a moment in 1970, so the session expires instantly. The caller wrote a number of seconds; the provider read a date. Providers differ - the contract must not.
cases: session ttl above the memcached thirty day boundary survives
session ttl at the memcached thirty day boundary survives
session ttl below the boundary still really expires
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-04 on the lab host (Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64) against a LIVE memcached 1.6.45, TINA4_REQUIRE_SERVICES=1, real wall-clock expiry with no clock mocking. This defect was UNANIMOUS across all four frameworks - a grep for 2592000 returned ZERO hits in python, php, ruby AND nodejs - which makes it a contract nobody had written down rather than four independent bugs. Re-measured directly against the real server before fixing anything: ttl=60 SURVIVES, ttl=2592000 SURVIVES, ttl=2592001 VANISHED INSTANTLY, ttl=4000000 VANISHED INSTANTLY. So TINA4_SESSION_TTL=2592001, an ordinary 'about a month' remember-me setting, was sent as the absolute stamp 1970-01-31, already past, and the item expired the instant it was stored; memcached still answers STORED, so the write looks successful and the very next read is a miss. A silent logout on every request, from a config value that looks perfectly reasonable. The fix CONVERTS a ttl past the boundary into the absolute stamp the protocol is asking for rather than CLAMPING to the ceiling, because clamping a 60-day session to 30 days silently shortens a lifetime the operator explicitly asked to lengthen - the same class of lie in the other direction. PHP additionally emitted the raw ttl from touch(); Ruby and Python have no touch in the session handler, which was checked rather than assumed. THE TEST DESIGN POINT WORTH KEEPING: a survival-only assertion CANNOT tell a conversion from a clamp, because both survive - so every framework's over-boundary case runs 2592001 AND 5184000 (60 days) and asserts the SERVER's own reported remaining ttl via a memcached meta-get on a socket the test owns, never through the code under test. MUTATION-PROVED in all four, each mutation asserted to APPLY before the run: removing the conversion reproduces the shipped defect ('a ttl of 2592001s expired the session instantly'), and replacing it with a CLAMP is caught ONLY by the 60-day case ('asked for a 5184000s session; the server says 2592000s remain'). Converting EVERY ttl to absolute correctly does NOT fail - that is a semantically equivalent implementation, merely more sensitive to client/server clock skew, and the test deliberately does not over-constrain it. Python 4772 passed / 27 skipped; PHP 4839 tests / 15295 assertions / 0 failures / 37 skipped; Ruby 4911 examples / 0 failures / 8 pending. OWED and deliberately out of scope here: the identical unclamped exptime exists in the CACHE memcached backend in all four frameworks - a different subsystem under a different contract fixture. A trap for whoever ports it there: Ruby's cache backend keeps local bookkeeping as `@own[k] = Time.now.to_f + exptime`, which would double-add if handed a converted absolute stamp and must take the caller's ttl instead.

invariants.rule: A backend that becomes unreachable mid-request is LOGGED and then degraded: the read yields an empty session, save() returns false, and the request still serves. It is never silent. TINA4_SESSION_STRICT re-raises instead.
invariants.why: MEASURED: in Python a session-backend failure on the real HTTP path is SILENT - request.session becomes None with nothing logged. An operator sees users mysteriously logged out and has no signal at all. A genuinely EMPTY session is not an error and must never be logged as one - that distinction is the whole point.
cases: a backend failure on the request path is logged not silent
a backend failure on the request path still serves the request
an empty session on the request path is not logged as a failure
strict mode on the request path refuses instead of degrading
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-04 on the lab host (Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64), TINA4_REQUIRE_SERVICES=1, against genuinely closed TCP ports and real Redis/PostgreSQL/SQLite. NO MOCKS: every case reads bytes the REAL logger wrote to a real file, each with a driver self-test so no log assertion can be vacuous. This invariant was owed on the REQUEST PATH specifically - all four already had a correct policy on the Session OBJECT, and all four failed to apply it where a Session is actually built. Each framework failed differently and each was WORSE than the original finding recorded. PYTHON: core/server.py:1404 was `except Exception: pass` with a comment claiming it covered a missing session module; it swallowed handler-construction failures, the deliberate unknown-backend ValueError, AND every strict-mode re-raise, so STRICT MODE WAS INERT. NODE: dispatchPipeline.ts:202-203 unguarded and save() unguarded inside the monkey-patched res.end while gc() four lines below WAS wrapped - and sessionAutoStart was called OUTSIDE the dispatch try, so the WORKER PROCESS DIED rather than returning 500. RUBY: session.rb:107 `@handler = create_handler` bare, plus a SECOND unguarded construction at rack_app.rb:1016 in the auth gate; measured pre-fix, unknown-backend, unreachable-database and strict mode all returned an identical 500, i.e. strict mode changed nothing observable. PHP: Router.php:670-672 constructed and started the Session with no try/catch at all. THE HALF MOST EASILY BROKEN, and the reason case 3 is not optional: a genuinely EMPTY session is NOT an error. A first-time visitor and a cookie for an unknown session are ordinary; logging them puts a line in the log for every new visitor and buries the real outage - the same blindness the fix was meant to cure. THREE DESIGN CORRECTIONS worth keeping. (a) Ruby's obvious fix - rescue inside Session#initialize - BROKE three existing examples that require an unknown backend to RAISE (the 2026-07-31 decision that a typo is a configuration error, not an outage); the fix ports Python's split instead, where Session raises and only the request path degrades. (b) Ruby cannot degrade to nil the way Python does: every session[...] in every app would become a NoMethodError and 500 the request the fix exists to save, so it degrades to an in-memory-only session whose reads are empty and whose save returns false. (c) Node's Tina4Request.session widens to `Tina4Session | null`, a type-level breaking change for app code doing req.session.get(...) - the old type was simply false, since after a degrade there is no session. MUTATION-PROVED in all four, each mutation asserted to APPLY before running: reverting the guard kills the loud/serves cases; dropping ONLY the strict re-raise kills EXACTLY the strict case; and an OVER-LOUD mutation that logs an empty read kills EXACTLY the empty-session control - that third one is what proves the control is a real gate rather than decoration. TWO near-misses recorded because they nearly produced false greens: in Ruby, mutating safe_read ALONE applies textually and fires NOWHERE (the request path resolves an empty session through existing_session_data, never through safe_read), and in Node case 1 SURVIVES the guard-only mutation because Node never had Python's silent-swallow mode - its honest kill is the full pre-fix pipeline, where the worker dies before it can answer. Python 4776 passed / 27 skipped; PHP 4843 tests / 15309 assertions / 0 failures / 37 skipped; Ruby 4915 examples / 0 failures / 8 pending; Node 7076 passed / 0 failed across 239 files, typecheck and build both exit 0.

invariants.rule: A session handler performs no network I/O in its constructor. Connection happens on first use, inside the log-loud-and-degrade policy.
invariants.why: MEASURED: the database backend does network I/O in the HANDLER CONSTRUCTOR, which sits OUTSIDE the failure policy. So the one place the policy cannot protect is the first thing that runs, and an unreachable backend takes the app down at construction rather than degrading per-request as designed.
cases: a session handler constructor performs no network io
the backend connection happens on first use not construction
a healthy backend still works after lazy connection
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-04 on the lab host (Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64), TINA4_REQUIRE_SERVICES=1, against live Redis 7, Valkey 8, memcached 1.6.45, MongoDB 7, PostgreSQL 16 and real SQLite. Broken in ALL FOUR at v3 HEAD, and in two of them worse than the original finding recorded. PYTHON: DatabaseSessionHandler.__init__ ran _ensure_table() - table_exists() + CREATE TABLE + commit(), real DDL on every request since the request path builds a Session per request - AND, NOT PREDICTED, MongoDBSessionHandler.__init__ called pymongo.MongoClient(url), which starts topology monitoring and DIALS IMMEDIATELY. The framework code looked lazy; the DRIVER was not. That one was caught only by the counting listener, which is the argument for the technique. PHP: DatabaseSessionHandler::__construct called Database::fromEnv(), and every Tina4 adapter constructor calls open() - pg_connect / mysqli / sqlsrv_connect / ibase_connect. RUBY: MongoHandler#initialize built a Mongo::Client then called ensure_ttl_index (a createIndexes round trip, and up to three network operations when it hits an IndexOptionsConflict and drops-and-recreates); DatabaseHandler#initialize constructed a Database and ran ensure_table. NODE: databaseHandler.ts:49-50 ran new DatabaseSync(dbPath) + PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL, which CREATES the .db plus its -wal and -shm siblings - three files on disk before a single session was read or written. THE PROOF TECHNIQUE IS THE POINT AND IS PORTED TO ALL FOUR: a real TCP server the test starts, which COUNTS accepted connections. Construct a handler pointed at it and the count must still be zero; do one operation and it must rise. It speaks no protocol and claims to be nothing, so it is a real server rather than a double, and the only thing it reports is a fact the KERNEL decided - a handler cannot connect without completing an accept() the test can see. No test double can answer that honestly. The database backends own no socket to watch, so they are measured by their SIDE EFFECT against a real engine instead (drop the table or the file, construct, and assert with a SECOND independent connection that it is still absent). CASE 2 IS THE ONE THAT STOPS A FALSE FIX: deferring the connection must not mean never connecting, because 'do no I/O in the constructor' is trivially satisfied by a handler that does no I/O at all. It earned its place - in Node it caught THREE separate ways case 1 was passing for the wrong reason, none of which review would have found: Atomics.wait BLOCKS the main thread so the listener's accept callback could never fire and the count could never rise; RedisSessionHandler reads redisHost/redisPort rather than host/port, so the wrong key was silently ignored and every construction dialled the REAL Redis on 6379 which the listener never saw; and the other three handlers DO use host/port, so one uniform config object is wrong for exactly one of the four. MUTATION-PROVED in all four, each mutation asserted present-exactly-once before replacing: putting the eager connect/DDL/open back in the constructor kills case 1 naming the backend, and making a handler INERT kills case 2 (and case 3 where the store is the same one). Python 4779 passed / 27 skipped; PHP 4846 tests / 15322 assertions / 0 failures / 37 skipped, run with --display-warnings and zero warnings; Ruby 4918 examples / 0 failures / 8 pending; Node 7079 passed / 0 failed across 240 files with typecheck and build both exit 0. OWED and stated rather than scoped out: Python's Database LAYER still connects in ITS own constructor, so Database() against a closed port raises rather than deferring. That is this same rule one level down, in a different subsystem under a different contract, and it is why the Python case measures the session handler's DDL side effect rather than its connect.

invariants.rule: A backend that advertises support for an engine works on that engine. The database session backend works on every engine the Database layer supports, not a subset.
invariants.why: MEASURED: Node's database session backend is SQLite-only and THROWS at Session construction on any other engine. Develop on sqlite, deploy on postgres, and the app does not start - the founding scenario of ADR-0024, in the subsystem that decides whether anyone is logged in.

invariants.rule: Where three frameworks ship a zero-dependency transport for a backend, the fourth does too. A backend must not hard-require a third-party client in one framework and not the others.
invariants.why: MEASURED: Ruby's mongodb session backend hard-requires the `mongo` gem while the other three ship a zero-dependency wire-protocol fallback. The same .env therefore works in three frameworks and raises in the fourth - and it breaks the zero-dependency promise asymmetrically, which is worse than breaking it consistently.
